# poseidon — design, sources & divergences (SPEC)

## Maturity

**Grade:** 3 · S2 E1 A1 H1 P3 · limited by performance (not measured) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** parity — iden3 circomlib / circomlibjs Poseidon (BN254, x^5, circom parameters) (surveyed 2026-09-30)

**Audit:** review 2026-08-06 · mutation 2026-11-14 (113/128, 15 eq) · src 3098fac768d7d959

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-07 (200,000 runs clean per harness, POSEIDON_FUZZ) · ct n/a — public-input hash (keyword review, 2026-10-07) · panic 2026-11-14 (sweep of every pub entry point: typed `Fr` and comptime widths leave no data path; LOW `mds_security.Checks` took a runtime `t` that indexed past fixed buffers above `n_max` and underflowed at 0, now a checked panic at all 9 entry points; LOW `grain.derive` looped forever on a zero modulus and dropped bits above 256, now `@compileError`)

**Performance:** ref 0.65–3.23× light-poseidon 0.4.0 (BN254 rows 0.65–0.75×) and neptune 14.0.0 (BLS12-381 rows 1.56–3.23×: its preprocessed sparse-matrix partial rounds and blst assembly; see Performance) · fastest ? (measured 2026-11-24; host shared with other jobs, best-of-rounds ratios repeat within 2 % across two runs)

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

Auditor/design reference. Consumer usage lives in `README.md`; metadata lives
in `src/root.zig`'s `pub const meta`; this file does not restate either.

**Where we are ahead:** of the Zig alternatives, the only Poseidon that reaches the deployed circom widths t = 2..17 and also covers BLS12-381, that derives its round constants from the authors' Grain-LFSR generator (with the MDS subspace-trail checks and rejection loop) instead of shipping a table, and whose permutation is built on constant-time field arithmetic. **Where we are behind:** no Poseidon2 (the direction newer ZK stacks are going); no variable-length sponge (a stated refusal, see *What is deliberately not done*); `bls12_381.Perm` only at t = 3 and 5 (Filecoin/neptune's arities 1..36 and domain tags are `poseidon.neptune`); field elements in and out (byte conversion is `bn254.Fr.toBytes`/`fromBytes` in the sibling), no `hash_bytes`-style convenience. (→ Backlog item: optimised partial rounds)

## What the hard part actually is

The permutation is twenty lines. Everything that decides *which numbers go in*
is the work, and it is where implementations diverge:

| decision | where it comes from here |
|---|---|
| round constants | `src/grain.zig`, ported from the authors' Grain-LFSR sage script |
| MDS matrix + its generation rule | same script's `create_mds_p` (Cauchy matrix) |
| `R_F` / `R_P` per field and width | `N_ROUNDS_P` / `N_ROUNDS_F`, copied from circomlib with its own provenance comment |
| S-box exponent `alpha` | fixed at 5; see below |

### `alpha = 5`, not 3

`x -> x^alpha` must be a bijection on `GF(p)`, i.e. `gcd(alpha, p-1) = 1`. For
both fields here `3 | p-1`, so `x^3` is not a bijection and `alpha = 5` is the
smallest admissible odd exponent. Both shipped parameter sets are `x^5`, and
every published vector is `x^5`. `x^-1` (the "Starkad/Poseidon over binary
fields" branch of the reference script) and `alpha = 3` are out of scope; the
Grain seed encodes the S-box choice, so adding one is a new parameter set with
new constants, not a flag.

## Sources

Primary, in the order they were consulted (neptune, the fourth source, is
the one `poseidon.neptune` follows):

1. **The paper** — *Poseidon: A New Hash Function for Zero-Knowledge Proof
   Systems*, Grassi/Khovratovich/Rechberger/Roy/Schofnegger,
   <https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/458>. Defines the HADES design strategy and
   the round-number analysis, but does **not** publish usable constants.
2. **The authors' reference code** — `hadeshash`,
   <https://extgit.iaik.tugraz.at/krypto/hadeshash> (redirects to
   `extgit.isec.tugraz.at`). `code/generate_parameters_grain.sage` is the
   constant generator this module ports; `code/poseidonperm_x5_25{4,5}_{3,5}.sage`
   are complete reference permutations with their constants inline;
   `code/test_vectors.txt` is the published KAT set.
3. **The deployed implementation** — `iden3/circomlib`
   (`circuits/poseidon.circom`, `circuits/poseidon_constants.circom`,
   and their `_old` counterparts) and `iden3/circomlibjs`
   (`src/poseidon_reference.js`, `src/poseidon_opt.js`,
   `src/poseidon_constants.json`). Both are copyleft — circomlibjs GPL-3.0,
   circomlib LGPL-3.0 — so they are consulted as behaviour, by being run, and
   nothing is copied out of them; see this module's `NOTICE`.

4. **Filecoin's Poseidon** — `neptune` (`filecoin-project` → `lurk-lab` →
   `argumentcomputer/neptune`; MIT OR Apache-2.0, `LICENSE-MIT` and
   `LICENSE-APACHE`, commit b06f03c5, 2025-03-10), read as source: `hash_type.rs`
   (domain tags), `round_numbers.rs` (its port of `calc_round_numbers.py`),
   `round_constants.rs` (the Grain call: field 1, **S-box tag 1**, `n = 255`),
   `mds.rs` (`M[i][j] = 1/(i + t + j)`), `poseidon.rs`/`poseidon_alt.rs` (the plain
   schedule, digest = state element 1) and its `hash_values` test. Its `NOTICE`
   entry names what is taken.

The paper and the deployed implementation **do not conflict on the function**.
They conflict on nothing that changes a digest, which was the thing worth
checking. The divergences that do exist are below.

## Divergences

### 1. Reference form vs optimized form — followed: reference, byte-compatible with both

circomlib ships Poseidon twice:

* `poseidon_old.circom` + `poseidon_constants_old.circom` — the plain HADES
  round structure, full round-constant table (195 values at `t = 3`), MDS used
  as `out[i] = Σ_j M[i][j]·in[j]`.
* `poseidon.circom` + `poseidon_constants.circom` — the *optimized* form
  (constant folding + sparse matrix factorisation): the round-constant table
  is folded down to `t·R_F + R_P` values (81 at `t = 3`), a pre-matrix `P` and
  `R_P` sparse matrices `S` replace most of the partial-round work, and the
  stored `M` is the **transpose**, consumed as `out[i] = Σ_j M[j][i]·in[j]`.

Verified in hand rather than assumed: `poseidon_constants_opt.json`'s `M[1]`
is exactly the transpose of `poseidon_constants.json`'s `M[1]`, and its `C[1]`
has 81 entries against the reference's 195.

**This module implements the reference form.** It is the one the paper
describes, the one the authors' sage scripts publish, and the one that can be
read. The optimized form is an arithmetic reorganisation for constraint count,
not a different function: circomlibjs' own test suite asserts
`poseidon_opt == poseidon_reference == poseidon_wasm` on every vector, and
`src/vectors_test.zig` independently matches values taken from *both* JS
implementations. If this module ever grows a circuit backend, the optimized
form is what it should emit — and the reference form is what would check it.

Nothing here is Poseidon2 (Grassi/Khovratovich/Schofnegger 2023), which is a
genuinely different permutation with a different linear layer. Not implemented (see *Backlog / deferred*).

### 2. `R_P` rounded up to a multiple of `t` — followed: circomlib

circomlib's own comment, in both `poseidon.circom` and
`poseidon_reference.js`:

> Using recommended parameters from whitepaper
> <https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/458.pdf> (table 2, table 8) / Generated by
> …/calc_round_numbers.py / **And rounded up to nearest integer that divides
> by t**

That last step is circomlib's, not the paper's. It only ever *adds* rounds, so
it is conservative — but it changes the Grain seed (`R_P` is one of the seeded
fields), so it changes every constant. Every value in `N_ROUNDS_P` is
divisible by its `t`; `constants_test.zig` asserts that, because it is the
fingerprint of this decision. Following the paper's unrounded table instead
would produce a hash no deployed circuit could verify.

### 3. Which state element the partial round's S-box hits — followed: `state[0]`

The reference sage permutations apply `state[0] = state[0]^5` in the partial
rounds, and circomlib does the same. Other ecosystems have used the last
element. This is not a matter of taste: it is a different permutation. Both
choices produce a deterministic hash that round-trips perfectly, which is
exactly why the published vectors are the only thing that settles it (see
*Anchoring*).

## Parameter generation

`grain.zig` is a faithful port of the sage script's GF(p) path, including the
two details that silently change the output:

* round constants are **rejection-sampled** (`while v >= p: redraw`), MDS seeds
  are **reduced** (`F(grain_random_bits(n))`). Using one rule for both
  desynchronises the stream.
* the Grain output filter consumes several clocks per emitted bit; it is not
  "one clock, one bit".

### The MDS rejection loop — reproduced

`mds_security.zig` carries the script's `algorithm_1`/`2`/`3` and
`check_minpoly_condition`, the subspace-trail tests of
Grassi-Rechberger-Schofnegger (<https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/500>), and
`derive` carries `generate_matrix`'s rejection loop around them.

Why it has to be there at all: a rejection is **not** a no-op. It consumes
another `2t` Grain draws, so every later value shifts. A generator without the
checks is silently wrong for any `(n, t, R_F, R_P)` where upstream happened to
reject a candidate — and it cannot tell you which parameter sets those are.
With them the generator can be pointed at a new parameter set without running
sage alongside.

For every parameter set shipped here the first candidate is the accepted one,
so **not one shipped table changed**. That is no longer prose: a
`constants_test.zig` case asserts `mds_candidates == 1` for all 18 of them,
alongside the digests that pin the values themselves.

#### How rare a rejection is, measured

`algorithm_3` rejects only when some ratio `λ_i/λ_j` of eigenvalues is a root
of unity of order at most `4t`. There are fewer than `(4t)^2` such roots and
`t(t-1)` ratios, so over a 254-bit prime the probability is about `2^-236`;
`algorithm_1` and `algorithm_2` need a rank-deficient `t x t` matrix, about
`1/p`. Empirically: a sweep of **816 BN254 parameter sets** (`t = 2..17`,
`R_P = 40..90`, `R_F = 8`) produced **zero** rejections.

That is a fine property for Poseidon and a bad one for a test suite — a check
that never fires is indistinguishable from `return true`. So the rejection
path is exercised over a small prime instead (`small_field.zig`,
`rejection_test.zig`). Over `p = 101`: 13 of 104 random matrices are rejected
and 5 of 48 `(t, R_P)` sets need more than one MDS candidate — enough that the
loop, its Grain-stream advance and `algorithm_1`'s sub-codes all get real
coverage.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class B · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class B** — published cryptographic or algorithmic construction with published vectors.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** circomlibjs JSON consts byte-identical (constants_test.zig)

Grade 1 (published vectors / reference-implementation output) throughout —
this repo's strongest tier. Two upstream sources, each with the exact
retrieval command recorded in `src/vectors_test.zig` and
`src/constants_test.zig`:

| what | source | covers |
|---|---|---|
| permutation KATs | `hadeshash/code/test_vectors.txt` | BN254 `t = 3, 5`; BLS12-381 `t = 3, 5` — all `t` output words |
| hash-framing KATs | circomlibjs *executed* (`tools/gen_vectors.mjs`), on the input sets upstream's own suite exercises | `Poseidon(1/2/4/6/16)`, non-zero initial state, multi-output |
| width sweep | circomlibjs *executed* (`poseidon_reference.js` and `poseidon_opt.js`, required to agree) | every `t = 2..17`, plus inputs at `r-1` |
| constants | `circomlibjs/src/poseidon_constants.json`; `hadeshash/code/poseidonperm_x5_25{4,5}_3.sage` | SHA-256 pins for all 18 shipped tables + literal spot values |
| neptune known answers | neptune's own `hash_values` test (read as source, `src/neptune_test.zig`) | Merkle-tag digests of inputs `0..arity` for arities 2, 4, 8, 11, 16, 24, 36 in both strengths; `ConstantLength(4)` for arities >= 4 |
| neptune parameters | neptune's `parameters/` directory (the authors' sage script output) | `round_numbers.txt` (`R_P` for every `t = 2..125`); the 585 arity-8 round constants (SHA-256 of the table) |
| neptune live run | neptune 14.0.0 (git b06f03c5) *executed* (`tools/oracle vectors`, frozen as `src/testdata/neptune_vectors.txt`) | 426 digests: all four hash types, both strengths, arities 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11, 16, 24, 36, three input sets each (small, full-size, zero) |

A **grade-2** cross-check also happened during development — an independent
Python port of the generator and the permutation, which reproduced every value
above — but it descends from the same sage script, so it is recorded as
corroboration and is not what the tests rest on. No grade-3 self round-trip is
used as an anchor anywhere.

#### The MDS security checks are grade 2 only, and here is why

There is no grade-1 anchor available for `algorithm_1`/`2`/`3`. The strongest
possible one would be a *published* parameter set whose accepted matrix is not
the first candidate: reproducing it byte-for-byte would prove both that the
checks fire and that ours fire in the same place. **No such set exists to
find.** Every published Poseidon-1 table generated by `create_mds_p` lives
over a 254/255-bit prime, where the rejection probability is `~2^-236` (see
above) — the 816-set sweep confirms it empirically for the whole circomlib
parameter space. Searched: circomlib/circomlibjs (`t = 2..17`, BN254),
`hadeshash`'s own `poseidonperm_x5_25{4,5}_{3,5}` sage files, and the
small-field ecosystems (Goldilocks/BabyBear in HorizenLabs' `poseidon2`,
Penumbra's `poseidon377`, Filecoin's `neptune`). The small-field ones do not
use `create_mds_p` at all — Poseidon2 builds its linear layer from
`generate_matrix_full`/`generate_matrix_partial`, and Penumbra states plainly
that it generates the Cauchy vectors *deterministically* (`x = 0..t-1`,
`y = t..2t-1`) rather than sampling, so no rejection loop runs there either.

What stands in its place, and what it is worth:

| evidence | what it does prove | what it does NOT |
|---|---|---|
| `constants_test.zig` — 18 shipped tables byte-identical to circomlib / the authors' sage, plus `mds_candidates == 1` | adding the checks changed nothing that is externally pinned | that a *rejection* is handled correctly — none occurs |
| `src/mds_replay_test.zig` + `src/testdata/mds_subspace_trail.txt` — 182 matrices over `GF(101)`/`GF(251)`/BN254 where rejections are common (19 of the 168 random ones), with an independent sympy port's verdict, **sub-code** and failing round captured per matrix and replayed with no Python | transcription fidelity, on inputs that actually fail, on every host | anything about a *shared misreading* of the sage source: both ports are ours |
| `rejection_test.zig` — `derive` over `GF(101)`, accepted matrix is the k-th draw and differs from the first | the loop advances the Grain stream, which is the failure mode that looks correct | — |
| the equivalence tests in `mds_security.zig` — fast path vs the literal transcription | the two `O(t^3)` rewrites (see that file) are not doing something else | — |

The sympy oracle is **not** external validation and is not described as such
anywhere. It is a second transcription of the same text by the same author; it
catches an index slip and it cannot catch a misread specification. sage is not
installed on the development host and installing it was out of scope.

**Where it runs.** The oracle is a program in `tools/`, not a
test: `tools/interop.zig` builds the 182 matrices, drives `tools/subspace_trail.py`
and writes what it said — matrix and verdicts, per case — into
`src/testdata/mds_subspace_trail.txt`, with the driver, the Python and sympy
versions, the capture date and the capture command in the header. The module's
own `src/mds_replay_test.zig` replays that transcript and spawns nothing, so the
comparison asserts on every host and cannot silently skip where sympy is
missing. The verdicts are a pure function of `(p, t, matrix)` — the four
algorithms take no randomness, time or environment — so the transcript needs no
determinism pinning beyond recording the matrices, which it does in full. The
replay regenerates every matrix from this module's own code and requires it to
equal the recorded one, and a coverage test pins the 12 batch names and the
total of 182, so the transcript cannot drift into pinning inputs nobody produces
or shrink quietly. Only the live program can see the *peer* change; that is what
`zig build interop-poseidon` is for, as a pre-release check.

### What the tests are built to separate

Poseidon's specific trap is that a wrong permutation is still a perfectly good
deterministic function: a partial-round S-box on the last element, a full S-box in
the partial rounds, a shifted round split with the same total round count, or a
wrong MDS-seed rule all leave the module compiling and every structural property
(invertible MDS, injectivity, determinism, framing consistency) intact. Only the
external vectors notice. Two consequences are built in. The constant pins separate
"the generator drifted" from "the permutation is wrong" (a digest mismatch names the
layer, e.g. `MDS digest mismatch at t=2`, while the round-constant digests stay
green). And the `t = 2..17` sweep exists because the three widths upstream's own
suite exercises are not enough: at `t = 5` no MDS seed draw happens to land above
`p`, so a generator that rejection-samples the seeds instead of reducing them is
invisible there.

A rejection that does not consume its Grain draw is the sharpest case on the
checks: it still yields a valid, invertible, MDS, perfectly deterministic matrix,
and no structural property notices. Only "the accepted matrix is the k-th draw
*and differs from the first*" does, which is why `rejection_test.zig` replays
`create_mds_p` by hand instead of trusting `derive`'s own output.

## Constant time

**Yes for the permutation, and it is meant to stay that way.**

`permute` has fixed loop bounds, no data-dependent branches, and no
memory access indexed by a data value. Every field operation comes from the
sibling `bn254`/`bls12_381` `Fr`, which is `std.crypto.ff`-backed constant-time
Montgomery arithmetic. `sbox` is `square/square/mul` — no exponentiation ladder,
no `pow`.

**Does it matter?** For the intended use, usually not: hashing public circuit
data leaks nothing. It does matter in three cases this module is expected to
serve, so the property is worth having rather than disclaiming:

* Merkle *membership* proofs, where the leaf and the path are the secret;
* commitments to witness values;
* Fiat-Shamir transcripts absorbing secret intermediates.

**Caveats, stated rather than left open:**

* `Perm(t).init()` — the Grain derivation — is emphatically *not* constant
  time (rejection sampling, a duplicate-scan loop, a variable-length modular
  inversion, and `mds_security`/`linalg`, whose control flow depends on
  ranks, polynomial degrees and factorisations). It consumes only public
  parameters, so this is fine, but do not reach for `grain.derive` or anything
  in `linalg.zig` with a secret.
* Unlike `k256` and `montint`, this module has **not** been CT-verified in the
  disassembly. The claim rests on the source shape plus `std.crypto.ff`'s own
  guarantees.

## Limits

- **Widths.** BN254: `t = 2..17` (1..16 inputs); anything else is a `@compileError`
  in `bn254.Perm` (`src/bn254_poseidon.zig`). BLS12-381: `t = 3` and `t = 5`
  only, `@compileError` otherwise. These are *policy* limits, not capability ones:
  there are no published parameters outside them, therefore no anchor, and with the
  rejection loop in place `grain.derive` reproduces upstream for any
  `(n, t, R_F, R_P)` without a sage run alongside. `mds_security.max_state_width`
  (17) is the only hard ceiling (`src/grain.zig`); raising it costs compile time
  and stack, nothing else.
- **Why BLS12-381 stops at `t = 3` and `t = 5`.** Upstream publishes reference
  scripts *and* test vectors for exactly those two widths over this field. There is
  no published `R_P` table for other widths and no deployed BLS12-381 Poseidon this
  could be byte-compatible with, so any other width would be an unanchored guess
  wearing the name of an anchored construction.
- **`bls12_381.Perm`'s framing is not anchored.** Only the **permutation** is
  externally anchored there. Its `hash`/`compress` framing (`[0] ++ inputs`, first
  output element) is this module's own, borrowed from the BN254 side; it does not
  match Filecoin's `neptune` (use `poseidon.neptune`) or dusk, which use domain
  tags. `bls12_381_poseidon.zig` says so at the call site.
- **`poseidon.neptune` arities.** `1..36` (neptune's `impl_arity!`: `U1..=U36`);
  `neptune.roundNumbers` is checked against its published table for every width
  `2..125`. Hash types: Merkle tree, constant length (up to the arity), encryption
  and custom ids `1..=256`. Sponge use (inputs longer than the arity) is not here,
  see *What is deliberately not done*.
- **Fixed arity.** `hash`/`hashN` take exactly `t - 1` inputs; there is no padding
  and no length encoding (`src/perm.zig`, `hashN`). `compress` exists only at
  `t = 3` and is a `@compileError` elsewhere.
- **`init()` is not constant time** and consumes only public parameters (see
  *Constant time*); an instance is immutable afterwards and is shared freely
  (`meta.concurrency = .reentrant`).
- **`init()` panics, `initChecked()` returns an error** for a `Config` whose MDS
  candidates keep getting rejected; that is unreachable for the shipped sets
  (`src/perm.zig`, `init`/`initChecked`).

## Performance

`zig build bench-poseidon` (`tools/bench.zig`, ReleaseFast, run under `hw run`)
times a chain of 16 dependent hashes, ours against light-poseidon 0.4.0
(`new_circom`, BN254) and neptune 14.0.0 (git b06f03c5, `OptimizedStatic`,
BLS12-381, standard strength), built offline from the pinned `Cargo.lock` in
`tools/oracle` (a foreign-crate review precedes the build: every `build.rs`
and proc-macro crate of the 95-package tree was read for network and out-of-tree
access; the only process spawns are `rustc --version` probes and the C compiler `cc`
runs for blst, the only file writes are into `OUT_DIR`). Both sides end every op on the same
digest (the count column), so the bench is also a cross-check. Two runs, 5 and 9
rounds, wall time, on a host shared with other jobs (spreads 5–74 %), best of
rounds each side:

| row | ours ns/op | reference ns/op | ours/ref (5 rounds, 9 rounds) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| `bn254_t3` (2 inputs) | 390 597 | 602 879 | 0.648, 0.655 |
| `bn254_t5` (4 inputs) | 975 648 | 1 292 588 | 0.755, 0.753 |
| `neptune_a2` | 390 427 | 251 134 | 1.555, 1.577 |
| `neptune_a4` | 932 012 | 424 403 | 2.196, 2.235 |
| `neptune_a8` | 2 794 915 | 848 304 | 3.295, 3.231 |

Against light-poseidon we are ahead (one op = 16 hashes: 24 µs per `t = 3` hash).
Against neptune we are behind and the gap grows with the width: neptune applies the
paper's optimised equivalent (the partial rounds as one sparse `O(t)` product,
constants folded forward), where `perm.zig` runs the plain `O(t²)` round; blst's
assembly field also helps. That gap is the Backlog item. Not measured: `init()`
alone, and neptune's other hash modes. For `init()`: `Perm(t).init()` runs the Grain LFSR once and then the MDS security checks,
and the checks dominate: about 70 000 field multiplications at `t = 17`, which is
70 ms at ReleaseSafe and 850 ms in Debug (`std.crypto.ff`'s constant-time multiply
costs about 0.8 us optimized and 9.6 us unoptimized). At `t = 3`, the case a Merkle
tree builds, it is about 2 ms optimized and 30 ms in Debug. Algorithmically the
checks are `O(t^3)`-ish rather than the `O(t^5)` a literal transcription costs;
`mds_security.zig` documents the two equivalences that buy that and the tests that
hold them. A consumer builds one instance per width and holds it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **Variable-length (sponge) hashing.** Poseidon's deployed use is fixed-arity:
  `Poseidon(n)` for a known `n`, which is what a circuit compiles to. A general
  sponge needs a padding rule and a domain-separation tag, and the deployed
  ecosystems do not agree on either (circomlib has none; Filecoin's `neptune` uses
  its own domain tags; other stacks use others). Adding one would mean shipping an
  unanchorable construction next to a set of byte-exact ones. If a caller needs it,
  `hashN` exposes the full permutation output, which is the primitive a duplex or
  sponge would be built from, but the convention should come from whatever it must
  interoperate with.
- **neptune's sponge API** (simplex/duplex absorb and squeeze, `ConstantLength(n)`
  with `n` above the arity, `HashType::Sponge`, the in-circuit gadgets, the GPU
  batch hasher and the tree builders). `poseidon.neptune` is the one-permutation
  hash (`Poseidon::hash`); a sponge would be a second, large construction with its
  own padding and IO-pattern rules, and the one-permutation digests are what a
  Filecoin tree or commitment needs. The `ConstantLength(4)` vector at arity 2 is
  skipped for that reason (it is a sponge over two blocks).
- **Circuit / constraint-system integration.** The optimized round structure
  (divergence 1) is what a future `groth16` gadget would want.
- **Widths outside the published ones**, see *Limits*.
- **The GF(2^n) / `x^-1` branch** of the reference script, and
  `generate_matrix_full` / `generate_matrix_partial`: those build Poseidon2's linear
  layer, which this module does not implement. `check_minpoly_condition` is ported
  anyway (it is one of the four checks and the natural companion to the other
  three) but it is not on the MDS generation path, exactly as upstream.
- **`alpha = 3` and the `x^-1` S-box**, see *`alpha = 5`, not 3*.
- **Rescue-Prime.** A separate design (every round full, alternating `x^alpha` and
  `x^(1/alpha)` layers), so not a mode of this module; it is the sibling module
  `rescue`, which shares no field with this one (the deployed variant uses
  Goldilocks `p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1`, so `rescue` carries its own small field).
- **Deriving the parameters at comptime.** Measured: the Zig interpreter costs
  about 18 us per LFSR clock, roughly 5 s for `t = 3` alone and about 200 s for the
  full sweep. That is why the tables live in an instance built by an ordinary
  function rather than in a `const`; `const P = comptime Perm(3).init();` works for
  a caller who prefers to pay compile time.
- **Marking the module `heavy`** (tests at ReleaseSafe in the Debug lane). Measured
  and rejected twice: the ReleaseSafe compile is 53 s against Debug's about 1 s, so
  the round trip gets longer, not shorter, and nothing depends on `poseidon`, so
  there is no second consumer to amortise that compile over. `std.crypto.ff`'s
  generic code is instantiated in whichever module calls it, which is why the
  already-`heavy` sibling field modules do not help.

## Verification

- **Run:** `scripts/modtest poseidon`; the Debug lane is slow (the checks are about 70 000 constant-time multiplications at `t = 17`, 9.6 us each unoptimized), `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast` is fast. The sympy peer is `zig build interop-poseidon` (re-run and diff, no rewrite) and `zig build interop-poseidon -- --capture` (re-take the transcript), a pre-release check.
- **Known answers:** the Poseidon authors' `test_vectors.txt` (BN254 and BLS12-381, `t = 3, 5`, every output word) and circomlibjs executed on the input sets upstream's suite exercises plus a `t = 2..17` sweep (`src/vectors_test.zig`, producer `tools/gen_vectors.mjs`).
- **neptune:** `src/neptune_test.zig`: neptune's `hash_values` known answers (both strengths, 7 arities), `round_numbers.txt` for `t = 2..125`, the arity-8 constants digest and its first and last constants, the Cauchy MDS, the domain tags, length checks, and the 426-line frozen live transcript (`src/testdata/neptune_vectors.txt`, regenerated by `tools/oracle`: `cargo build --release --offline --locked`, then `poseidon-oracle vectors`). `zig build bench-poseidon` is the performance run.
- **Constants:** SHA-256 pins for all 18 shipped tables plus literal spot values, and `mds_candidates == 1` for every shipped set (`src/constants_test.zig`).
- **MDS security checks:** the transcript replay (`src/mds_replay_test.zig`, 12 batch names, 182 matrices, no `python3`), the rejection-loop tests over a small prime (`src/rejection_test.zig`, `src/small_field.zig`), the fast-path-versus-literal equivalence tests in `src/mds_security.zig`, and `src/linalg.zig`'s own tests.
- **Fuzz:** `src/fuzz_test.zig`, injectivity harnesses for the BN254 and BLS12-381 `t = 3` permutation with a pinned seed corpus, run by the deterministic driver (`POSEIDON_FUZZ`). The card's Hardening line has the run.
- **ct:** n/a for the hash (public inputs by intent); the permutation is constant time by source shape, not verified in the disassembly (*Constant time*).
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it. Not mutated: the comptime round-count tables (pinned by `constants_test.zig`), checked panics, cost-only zero skips. The equivalent mutants are the 64-rejection attempt cap, guards subsumed by a later one, a never-read slot, constant-polynomial guards and primality/Rabin conditions.

## Backlog / deferred

- **Optimised partial rounds** (measured gap to neptune: 1.56× at 2 inputs, 3.2× at 8). The paper's equivalent
  form: fold the round constants forward through the MDS inverse and replace each partial round's `t × t` product
  with a sparse one (first row and column plus a diagonal), `O(t)` per round instead of `O(t²)` over the `R_P`
  partial rounds; neptune does exactly this (`preprocessing.rs`, `matrix.rs`). The output must stay byte-identical
  to the plain schedule (the existing vectors and the neptune transcript are the test). Moderate; the
  per-width precomputation goes into `init()`.

## Roadmap

- **Poseidon2.** The newer ZK stacks (Plonky3, gnark-crypto, HorizenLabs, and the Zig `blockblaz/zig-poseidon`) ship Poseidon2, not the original permutation, and a user coming from them finds no digest here. It is a different permutation with its own linear layer, parameter set and vectors, a scoping note and not a refusal, so it stays a backlog candidate. Sizeable (new linear layer, `generate_matrix_full/partial` from the same sage script, vectors per field); published vectors exist for it. Fits CONVENTIONS section 2 (pure Zig; the fields are the sibling `bn254`/`bls12_381` and, for Goldilocks, `rescue`'s in-module field).
  Project-size: a second permutation family (linear layers, round constants per field from the sage script, vectors
  for BN254, BLS12-381 and Goldilocks), weeks.
